title: Antipsychotic medication for psychosis
description: Antipsychotic medication is the main treatment for psychosis; all effective antipsychotics act on the striatum, deep in the brain. One study scanned people at rest during a first episode of psychosis, before and after 12 weeks of treatment. As psychosis improved, the striatum worked more closely with the front of the brain and with emotional and memory areas, and less closely with the parietal lobe. Lines show the change in how closely areas work together: pulsing means more than before, dashed means less than before.
caveat: All findings come from one study of 24 people in a first episode of psychosis, treated with risperidone or aripiprazole, and 24 people without psychosis scanned twice. The changes are those that went with improvement in psychosis, at rest; they show how closely areas work together, not activity. The striatum is drawn as the caudate because the source names "striatal regions" without saying which; that is an assumption. The source names the anterior cingulate and the parietal lobe without saying which parts; they are drawn on the dorsal anterior cingulate and the inferior parietal cortex. These are averages across groups of people, not a picture of any one person's brain. Treatments help many people, not everyone, and in different ways. This is not medical advice: talk to a doctor or therapist about what is right for you.
